auditor_notes: Fact base: Folger Shakespeare Library text, MIT Shakespeare, SparkNotes, LitCharts, RSC, eNotes. All 30 lessons across AQA (7), Edexcel (7), OCR (8), Eduqas (8) audited for factual accuracy in quotes, scene/act attribution, character actions, plot chronology. Thematic interpretation not flagged. Issues only: lessons with no errors are listed with an empty issues array.

lessons.title: Act 3: Hath Not a Jew Eyes?

issues.claim: "Salarino and Solanio taunt Shylock about Jessica's elopement."
issues.correct: In Act 3 Scene 1, the two characters who taunt Shylock are Solanio and Salerio — not Salarino. Salarino appears in Acts 1–2; in Act 3 Scene 1 the Folger text and most scholarly editions name the second character as Salerio (a messenger from Venice, distinct from Salarino). Using 'Salarino' for Act 3 Scene 1 is the wrong character name.
issues.recommended_fix: Replace 'Salarino and Solanio' with 'Salerio and Solanio' in the Act 3 Scene 1 discussion.

issues.location: Jessica's elopement section — Shylock's reported speech
issues.claim: Lesson presents 'I would my daughter were dead at my foot and the jewels in her ear!' as something Shylock says in Act 3 Scene 1.
issues.correct: This is reported speech — Solanio is recounting (and mocking) what Shylock was heard saying in the streets. Shylock does not deliver this line directly on stage in Act 3 Scene 1. The lesson's phrasing frames it as a direct speech act, which slightly misrepresents how the line reaches the audience. Similarly, 'My daughter! O my ducats!' is Solanio's reported mockery of Shylock (Act 2 Scene 8), not an on-stage line.
issues.recommended_fix: Clarify that 'I would my daughter were dead at my foot...' is reported by Solanio as something Shylock said off-stage, rather than a line Shylock speaks directly in Act 3 Scene 1.

issues.claim: "Portia arrives disguised as a young male lawyer named Balthazar, sent by the legal scholar Doctor Bellario to adjudicate the case."
issues.correct: Bellario is Portia's cousin (established in Act 3 Scene 4) and is a Doctor of Laws based in Padua — not simply a 'legal scholar'. More importantly, Portia was not 'sent' by Bellario; she devised the plan herself and used Bellario's credentials and letter as cover. Bellario's letter introduces 'Balthazar' as a young doctor of Rome who has studied the case with Bellario. The lesson's phrasing 'sent by Bellario' misrepresents who originates the plan.
issues.recommended_fix: Change to something like: 'Portia arrives disguised as the young lawyer Balthazar, armed with a letter from her cousin Doctor Bellario of Padua, whose credentials give her access to the court.'

issues.location: Opening paragraph on the 'Hath not a Jew eyes?' speech
issues.claim: "When Solanio and Salerio taunt Shylock about Antonio's failing fortunes, Shylock responds with..."
issues.correct: In Act 3 Scene 1, Salerio and Solanio taunt Shylock primarily about Jessica's elopement — not primarily 'Antonio's failing fortunes'. Salerio does mention a rumour about a ship loss when Shylock asks about Antonio, but the sustained taunting that triggers the 'Hath not a Jew eyes?' speech concerns Jessica. The news of Antonio's ships is confirmed separately by Tubal later in the same scene. Misidentifying the trigger as 'Antonio's failing fortunes' misrepresents the dramatic context of the speech.
issues.recommended_fix: Change 'taunt Shylock about Antonio's failing fortunes' to 'taunt Shylock about Jessica's elopement'. The separate confirmation of Antonio's ship losses (from Tubal) can be mentioned as a subsequent development in the same scene.

issues.claim: The lesson quotes 'If he have the condition of a saint and the complexion of a devil, I had rather he should shrive me than wive me' and positions it as Portia's reaction in the Morocco scenes.
issues.correct: This line is from Act 1 Scene 2, where Portia is talking to Nerissa about her suitors before Morocco arrives. The lesson's framing places it as if it follows Morocco's failed choice, but it is spoken before Morocco's first entrance. It is still a line about Morocco specifically, but its placement in the lesson narrative implies it comes after the casket scene rather than before it.
issues.recommended_fix: Clarify that this line is from Act 1 Scene 2 (Portia's conversation with Nerissa about suitors before Morocco arrives), not a reaction to his failed casket choice.

issues.correct: The standard historical/scholarly form is 'Roderigo Lopez'. 'Rodrigo' is a variant used in some popular sources but 'Roderigo Lopez' is the form used in most GCSE-level and academic sources when discussing The Merchant of Venice's context.

lessons.title: Acts 2-3: Hath Not a Jew Eyes?

issues.claim: "Shylock, taunted by Salarino and Solanio about Jessica's elopement..."
issues.correct: In Act 3 Scene 1 (Folger and most scholarly editions) the two characters are Solanio and Salerio — not Salarino. Salarino appears in Acts 1–2 but is a different character from Salerio. Using 'Salarino' for Act 3 Scene 1 is the wrong character name.
issues.recommended_fix: Replace 'Salarino and Solanio' with 'Salerio and Solanio'.

issues.location: Description of Marlowe's Barabas in The Jew of Malta
issues.claim: "a cartoonish villain who poisons wells and murders nuns."
issues.correct: Barabas does not poison wells in The Jew of Malta. He poisons a convent of nuns (via a pot of rice/porridge). The 'poisons wells' detail is factually wrong — this is a different common anti-Semitic trope (blood libel / well-poisoning) that does not feature in Marlowe's play.
issues.recommended_fix: Change 'poisons wells and murders nuns' to 'poisons a convent of nuns and orchestrates a series of murders'.

lessons.title: Act 3: Hath Not a Jew Eyes?

cross_board_issues.description: Character name 'Salarino' used for Act 3 Scene 1 in AQA L3 and OCR L3
cross_board_issues.correct_form: In Act 3 Scene 1, the standard Folger and most scholarly editions name the two characters as Solanio and Salerio (not Salarino). Salarino appears in Acts 1–2; Salerio is the messenger from Venice who appears in Act 3 Scene 1. Edexcel L3 and Eduqas L3 both correctly use 'Salerio'.
cross_board_issues.recommended_fix: In AQA L3 and OCR L3, replace 'Salarino' with 'Salerio' in the Act 3 Scene 1 discussion.

cross_board_issues.description: Lopez name variant across context lessons — OCR L1 uses 'Rodrigo', others use 'Roderigo'
cross_board_issues.correct_form: Standard scholarly/GCSE form is 'Roderigo Lopez'. All other board lessons use 'Roderigo Lopez' correctly. OCR L1 alone uses 'Rodrigo Lopez'.
cross_board_issues.recommended_fix: In OCR L1, change 'Rodrigo Lopez' to 'Roderigo Lopez'.

cross_board_issues.description: Trigger for 'Hath not a Jew eyes?' speech misidentified in Edexcel L3
cross_board_issues.correct_form: The speech is provoked by Salerio and Solanio taunting Shylock about Jessica's elopement. The confirmation of Antonio's ship losses comes separately from Tubal later in the same scene. Edexcel L3 identifies 'Antonio's failing fortunes' as the trigger, which is inaccurate.
cross_board_issues.recommended_fix: In Edexcel L3, change the trigger to 'taunted about Jessica's elopement'. The Antonio ship news from Tubal can be noted as a separate development in Act 3 Scene 1.

cross_board_issues.description: Marlowe's Barabas 'poisons wells' — wrong detail in Eduqas L1 only
cross_board_issues.correct_form: In The Jew of Malta, Barabas poisons a convent of nuns (not wells). 'Poisons wells' is a different anti-Semitic blood-libel trope not present in Marlowe's play. Other board lessons describe Barabas more accurately as poisoning nuns.
cross_board_issues.recommended_fix: In Eduqas L1, change 'poisons wells and murders nuns' to 'poisons a convent of nuns and orchestrates a series of murders'.

key_findings: The 30 lessons are broadly factually accurate. No errors were found in: the three key speeches and their attribution (Hath not a Jew eyes = Shylock Act 3 Scene 1; The quality of mercy = Portia Act 4 Scene 1; In Belmont is a lady richly left = Bassanio Act 1 Scene 1); casket inscriptions and suitor outcomes (Morocco/gold/skull, Arragon/silver/fool, Bassanio/lead/portrait); the turquoise ring and Leah detail; the trial loophole mechanism; Shylock's punishment terms and forced conversion; the ring plot structure in Act 5; core character descriptions and relationships.

The only HIGH severity issue is Edexcel L3 misidentifying the immediate trigger for Shylock's 'Hath not a Jew eyes?' speech as 'Antonio's failing fortunes' rather than the taunting about Jessica's elopement.

A recurring MEDIUM issue: AQA L3 and OCR L3 use the character name 'Salarino' for the Act 3 Scene 1 scene, when the correct name for that character in standard editions is 'Salerio'. Edexcel and Eduqas correctly use 'Salerio'.
AQA L4 mildly misrepresents the Portia/Bellario relationship: says she was 'sent by Bellario' when she devised the scheme herself and used Bellario's letter as cover.

Edexcel L4 quotes Portia's 'If he have the condition of a saint...' line in a context that implies it follows Morocco's casket failure, when the line is actually spoken in Act 1 Scene 2 before Morocco arrives.

Eduqas L1 contains a minor contextual error about The Jew of Malta: Barabas 'poisons wells' should be 'poisons a convent of nuns'. Well-poisoning is a different (blood-libel) trope not in Marlowe's play.
OCR L1 uses 'Rodrigo Lopez' rather than the standard 'Roderigo Lopez'.
